newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria oil refinery curbs fuel distribution.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria oil refinery curbs fuel distribution.

text.p: Bulgaria's biggest oil refinery Neftohim, plagued by losses, said on Thursday it had imposed limits to its fuel deliveries for the domestic market due to crude shortages.

The state-owned Neftohim refinery in Bourgas, which normally supplies more than 70 percent of the domestic market, will reduce its deliveries of petrol and diesel to 1,000 tonnes per day, plant spokeswoman Tatyana Hadzhieva said.

Since Monday the refinery has sold 1,000 tonnes of petrol per day, 2,000 tonnes of diesel oil and 3,000 tonnes of naphtha, officials said. In winter the refinery usually sells 2,500-3,000 tonnes of petrol per day.
Neftohim said it has been refining only 8,000 tonnes of crude per day since Monday, while its capacity is 25,000 tonnes.
The refinery, which posted losses of 100 billion levs last year and 37 billion levs in January, has only one distillation unit running instead of the normal three.
A 65,000-tonne crude tanker arrived at Bourgas on Wednesday from Russia's port of Odessa. Now Neftohim has some 80,000 tonnes of crude in stock, Hadzhieva said.
But it was unclear how often oil suppliers would deliver crude to the Bourgas refinery which lacks cash, officials said.
Russia's state-owned Rosneft oil company said on Tuesday it had cut crude oil supplies to Neftohim because of unpaid debts.
On Thursday some service stations were closed due to a lack of fuel and those open were limiting the amounts that customers could buy.
Motorists said they had queued for an hour and were limited to 20 litres of gasoline.
Shell Bulgaria, a Royal Dutch/Shell group subsidiary and the only foreign fuel retailer in Bulgaria, said they were dependent on Neftohim, which is its only gasoline supplier in Bulgaria.

Neftohim's management has complained many times of low domestic prices and the drastic fall of the lev to the dollar. The plant purchases its crude at international spot market prices in hard currency while domestic fuel prices are several times lower than production costs, refinery officials say. -- Liliana Semerdjieva, Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
